source_evidence.quote: Our initial investigation (Findling et al., 2023 ) used data from an NIMH-funded double-masked randomized study with three active treatment arms (Sikich et al., 2008 ). We identified five factors on the PANSS that aligned with those found in adult patients: Withdrawal/Apathy, Thought Disturbance, Aggression, Internalizing, and Delusions/Odd Content. Further investigation in that sample and in additional independent, randomized, placebo-controlled double-blind trial data (Busner et al., 2024 ; Youngstrom et al., 2024 ) replicated this factor structure and found further evidence of favorable psychometric properties for two optimized versions of the PANSS: a 20-item version (PANSS20), which eliminates the least informative items from the original PANSS; and a 10-item form (PANSS10) that focuses on the two most informative items from each factor. Further work has provided evidence that both the PANSS10 and PANSS20 attain excellent coverage of content from the 30-item version, as well as very good reliability, sensitivity to treatment, and evidence of criterion validity (Busner et al., 2024 ; Findling et al., 2023 ; Youngstrom et al., 2024 ). The PANSS10 shows particular promise as a clinical outcome assessment, demonstrating equivalent ability to detect treatment effects compared with the PANSS30 with substantially fewer items (see: Youngstrom et al., 2024 ).

source_evidence.role: report chain: self-report versus later costly behavior
source_evidence.quote:
Classic ISE research has focused on inconsequential self-reports, leaving open whether encountering outgroup criticism has behavioural consequences. Viewing the maintenance of a positive group identity as a goal (cf. Gollwitzer et al., 1982) allows conceiving of a threat to positive group identity as an obstacle to goal attainment. In general, threats to goal attainment lead to increasing effort (Carver & Scheier, 1990;Thürmer et al., 2020). Thus, when outgroup criticism threatens the goal of maintaining a positive social identity, group members should actively defend this identity (cf. Baumeister & Scher, 1988;Crocker & Park, 2004) and express their sensitivity to intergroup criticism in costly behaviour (behavioural ISE).
In line with this view, Thürmer and McCrea (2018) observed that group members paid to punish critical outgroup comments, excluded outgroup commenters from a subject pool, and rejected ultimatum bargaining offers from outgroup commenters, compared with ingroup commenters voicing the same criticism.

To ensure a stringent test of our hypotheses, we followed the procedures by Thürmer and McCrea (2018, Experiment 3) very closely.

Our experimental setup therefore provided a stringent test of the expected effects.

source_evidence.quote:
In line with this general norm explanation, Sutton et al. (2006) observed the ISE even among uninvolved bystanders who were members of a third group (bystander ISE). Although these results are impressive and based on the same materials used in existing ISE research, there was no direct comparison between the classic ISE conditions (i.e., criticism targeted at one's own ingroup) and bystanders (i.e., criticism targeted at another group) in this study. Sutton et al. (2008) included such a comparison and found consistent evidence for both the classic ISE and the bystander ISE, with both effects being of similar magnitude.
Although their sample was sufficient to detect a medium-sized interaction, it did not provide sufficient power to detect a small effect. Given that interactions are typically smaller than main-effects, a high-powered test of this effect is warranted.

To ensure a stringent test of our hypotheses, we followed the procedures by Thürmer and McCrea (2018, Experiment 3) very closely.

Our experimental setup therefore provided a stringent test of the expected effects.

reviewed_current_coding_originals.evidence_quote: We conducted additional exploratory tests to determine whether identification with the ingroup could account for the observed results. In particular, it is possible we did not observe more support for the social identity account because participants were not sufficiently identified with the ingroup. We therefore examined whether the classic and bystander ISE effects were consistent across levels of identification. In line with previous research (Thürmer et al., 2019), Johnson-Neyman Analyses indicated that the behavioural classic ISE on participants' bonus payment decision was significant for those participants reporting medium-tohigh identification with their group (2.45 and above), but not for those reporting low identification (Figure 1a). 1 The bystander ISE was significant at all levels of identification (Figure 1b). In contrast, the behavioural bystander ISE was observed across levels of ingroup identification. We observed a parallel pattern of results for reported message threat, though not for message motive.

source_evidence.quote:
To ensure a stringent test of our hypotheses, we followed the procedures by Thürmer and McCrea (2018, Experiment 3) very closely.
We used the same established manipulation for the classic ISE, selfreport measures that are used widely in ISE research (Hornsey & Imani, 2004), and the same behavioural measure. We only adapted the paradigm to include the two bystander ISE conditions, to measure message constructiveness before the message threat to provide a better exploratory process test, and added a four-item measure of group identification (adapted from Thürmer et al., 2019) after the behavioural measure. Our experimental setup therefore provided a stringent test of the expected effects.
